name: Spermidine
lead: Spermidine is a naturally occurring polyamine (C7H19N3) found in all living cells, first isolated from semen, and present in foods such as wheat germ, soybeans, mushrooms and aged cheese [1][2][3]. It is a precursor to spermine and takes part in cell growth, membrane function and RNA and DNA stabilisation [1]. It is sold as an oral supplement, often as wheat germ extract, and is promoted as an autophagy-inducing longevity compound [4][5].

Its profile rests largely on laboratory and animal work. A 2009 Nature Cell Biology paper reported that spermidine extended lifespan in yeast, flies, worms and human immune cells through autophagy, and a 2016 Nature Medicine paper reported cardioprotection and lifespan extension in mice [6][7]. Observational data link higher dietary polyamine intake with lower cardiovascular and cancer-related mortality, but randomised human trials remain few and small, and no study has shown a cosmetic benefit in people [4][8][9].

Wikipedia also notes a laboratory finding that spermidine promoted hair shaft elongation in cultured hair follicles; this has not been established in clinical hair-growth trials [1]. In bodybuilding forums spermidine is discussed as a longevity hack, typically via wheat germ [2][10].

paras: Spermidine is an aliphatic polyamine. In plants and some bacteria it is formed from putrescine by spermidine synthase, and it is the precursor of spermine and thermospermine; some gut bacteria make it through a different two-enzyme route [1]. Cellular levels are tightly regulated, and reviews state that polyamine levels decline with age and are altered in some diseases, including Parkinson's disease [11][6]. Gut microbial production and dietary intake both contribute to the body's supply [12][13].

Chemically, spermidine is a linear triamine with two terminal primary amines and one internal secondary amine, systematically named N-(3-aminopropyl)butane-1,4-diamine, with a molar mass of about 145 g/mol.[30] In cells it is built from putrescine by transfer of an aminopropyl group from decarboxylated S-adenosylmethionine, and it is the precursor of spermine.[30][1] Because it carries positive charge at physiological pH, it binds nucleic acids and helps stabilise DNA and RNA and support transcription and translation.[30]

Wikipedia describes spermidine as a regulator of membrane potential, intracellular pH and cell volume, and notes effects on calcium influx through NMDA-type glutamate receptors and on neuronal nitric oxide synthase.[1] Grokipedia states that the highest concentrations in the human body are in the brain, particularly white matter, and that levels fall with age across species.[30] Reviews of polyamine biology describe the three polyamines as abundant polycations needed by essentially all mammalian cells, with levels controlled by synthesis, degradation, uptake and export.[11]

Outside nutrition, spermidine is a routine reagent in molecular biology. Wikipedia lists its use in electroporation when moving DNA into cells, in purifying DNA-binding proteins, in precipitating DNA onto microprojectiles for gene-gun delivery, in in vitro transcription and translation reactions, and in improving the specificity of Taq-based PCR by stabilising the charge on the DNA backbone.[1] The pure laboratory chemical carries a corrosive hazard classification, which is separate from the low intakes found in food and supplements.[1]

Wikipedia gives a table of spermidine content in foods, in milligrams per kilogram: wheat germ about 243, dried soybean about 207 (Japanese data) or 128 (German data), one-year-old cheddar about 199, mushroom about 89, rice bran about 50, chicken liver about 48, green peas about 46, mango about 30, chickpea about 29, and cooked cauliflower and broccoli about 25. Wikipedia adds that grain endosperm holds most of the spermidine in cereals, content varies by source and age, and the Mediterranean diet is described as rich in it.[1]
For comparison, Wikipedia lists human seminal plasma at about 15 to 50 mg per litre. It also notes that many gut bacteria lack spermidine synthase and use a two-enzyme route instead.[1]

Spermidine in the body comes from three routes: the diet, synthesis by the body's own cells, and production by gut bacteria.[12][13] A 2024 review in Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition covers the link between polyamine metabolism, the microbiome and ageing, and discusses probiotics and prebiotics that might support spermidine supply.[12] A Trends in Cell Biology review describes spermidine as produced by combined bacterial pathways, bacteria-host co-metabolism, and activated immune cells, and reports that in aged animals it improved responses to anti-PD-1 cancer immunotherapy.[13] In diet-induced obese mice, spermidine supplementation improved gut barrier integrity and microbiota function.[23]

Autophagy is the cell's recycling system for damaged proteins and organelles, and a 2011 review in Cell described how genetic inhibition of autophagy in mammals produces degenerative changes resembling ageing and how many life-extending manipulations in model organisms stimulate it.[31] That framing is the backdrop to spermidine's reputation: it is one of several compounds described as caloric restriction mimetics, agents proposed to reproduce some benefits of dietary restriction without the restriction itself.[4] The 2018 Science review lists reported cardioprotective, neuroprotective and anticancer-immunosurveillance effects in rodents and notes that spermidine is already part of daily nutrition, which makes trials that raise intake feasible.[4] A 2022 Nature Aging review sets out the molecular mode of action, including the acetylation-related and eIF5A hypusination pathways, and the questions that remain for clinical translation.[5]
A 2024 Cell Metabolism overview of human trials of anti-ageing interventions places spermidine among agents whose human testing is at an early stage.[32]

Spermidine was originally isolated from semen, which gave the compound its name [1]; a 1976 Annual Review of Biochemistry article reviewed the biochemistry of putrescine, spermidine and spermine [14]. Interest in longevity grew after a 2009 report that spermidine induces autophagy and promotes longevity in several organisms [6], followed by mouse cardioprotection data in 2016 [7] and a 2018 Science review framing spermidine as a caloric restriction mimetic [4]. A 2021 study reported that dietary spermidine improved cognitive function in fruit flies and related models [15].

Wikipedia reports that spermidine lengthened hair shafts and upregulated epithelial stem cell-associated keratins K15 and K19 in laboratory hair-follicle models [1]. No clinical trial of oral or topical spermidine for hair growth or skin appearance has been reported. A registered gel trial uses spermidine for peri-implant mucositis rather than cosmetic outcomes [16].

The laboratory work cited is a 2011 PLOS ONE paper by Ramot, Tiede, Biro and colleagues, which tested human hair follicles and cells in vitro and in situ and reported dose-dependent effects on K15 promoter activity, colony-forming efficiency, proliferation and K15 expression alongside longer hair shafts.[29][1]

In the hair-follicle study, the reported readouts were longer hair shafts in organ culture and altered activity of epithelial stem cell markers in isolated cells; they were laboratory measurements, and the authors framed spermidine as a modulator of epithelial stem cell function.[29] Wikipedia also mentions that fertile men are reported to have higher spermidine levels than infertile men and that spermidine has been linked to fertility, a statement the Wikipedia article itself flags as needing better medical citation.[1]
Spermidine has been studied for cognition, hypertension, vaccine response in older adults, coronary artery disease, lipids and obesity, and radiation-induced dry mouth [8][17][18][19][20][21][22].

Autophagy is the main proposed mechanism: spermidine is reported to inhibit the acetyltransferase EP300, raising acetylation of tubulin and promoting autophagy, and possibly to act through the MAPK pathway [1][5]. Spermidine also supports hypusination of eIF5A, linked to mitochondrial function and immune cell activity, and reviews describe effects on inflammation, lipid metabolism and the gut barrier [5][13][23][1]. Cardioprotection in mice involved enhanced cardiac autophagy and mitophagy [7].

A small registered study examined bioavailability of spermidine in healthy men, and an exploratory randomised trial in older men found that 40 mg per day had minimal effects on circulating polyamines [24][9].

A randomised clinical trial in older adults with subjective cognitive decline, published in JAMA Network Open in 2022, tested longer-term spermidine supplementation on memory performance and biomarkers [8]. A 2026 pilot randomised study in healthy older adults examined effects on immune cell senescence and vaccine responses [18], and a registered trial examined spermidine-induced autophagy and COVID-19 vaccination [19]. An exploratory trial in older men found minimal changes in circulating polyamines at 40 mg per day [9], and a pilot dose-escalation study tested a fasting-mimetic blend including spermidine in healthy young men [25].

Registered trials include studies on hypertension, blood lipids in overweight individuals, polyamine treatment in elderly coronary artery disease, metabolic responses in healthy adults, and healthy-ageing biomarkers [17][21][20][26][27]. A cohort study related plasma polyamines to short-term outcomes after ischaemic stroke [28]. Reviews note that most evidence comes from cell and animal studies, and that human randomised data are preliminary [4][5].

Wikipedia notes that its cited human data are observational: in one analysis spermidine intake was correlated with lower blood pressure, and it reports no clinical trial results in humans on its own page.[1] No clinical trial of spermidine for hair or skin appearance has been published.

Trial registrations give a sense of the field's current size: a Phase 3 hypertension study listed with 46 participants, a Phase 2 trial in elderly coronary artery disease patients listed as completed with 187, a bioavailability study in 6 healthy men, a 42-person metabolic-response study, a 40-person vaccination study and a 20-person peri-implant mucositis gel study, plus recruiting studies on radiation-induced dry mouth (58) and blood lipids in overweight adults (50).[17][20][24][26][19][16][22][21] An iterative design trial of ageing-targeted supplements and a healthy-ageing biomarker study are also registered.[33][27] The cognitive trial and the 2026 pilot are the principal published randomised human reports.[8][18]

Human trials of oral spermidine have generally reported good tolerability at studied intakes, with mild gastrointestinal effects possible [8][9]. Polyamines are needed by rapidly dividing cells, and reviews discuss both anticancer immune effects and the theoretical possibility of supporting tumour growth in some contexts [4][13]. A review on polyamines in Parkinson's disease describes both neuroprotective and neurotoxic effects depending on context [11].

T Nation writers have promoted wheat germ as a food source and described spermidine as a longevity compound shown in animals to extend lifespan by as much as 25 percent, while noting the joke-prone name and that supplements exist [2][10]. A calorie-restriction article lists it alongside resveratrol as a longevity compound [3].

Online discussion has been modest in volume. Hacker News threads titled around whether spermidine is a legitimate anti-ageing supplement and around the 2018 Science review had a few points and no comments.[34][35] T Nation's longevity pieces are the clearest bodybuilding-community coverage; the author of one calls spermidine a hack he was currently enthusiastic about while acknowledging its joke-prone name.[10] An older T Nation thread on agmatine, a related arginine metabolite, cites literature on agmatine's modulation of polyamine content in liver cells, showing the compound family has long been discussed in supplement circles.[36]

Spermidine is sold as a dietary supplement, most commonly as wheat germ extract, and is treated as a supplement or novel food in many regions; regulatory treatment differs by jurisdiction.[4][5] Supplement marketing generally frames it around healthy ageing and autophagy, the language used in the scientific reviews.[5]

lore.intro: Spermidine is discussed in training forums as a longevity and autophagy supplement, usually via wheat germ extract [2][10].

claims.claim: Spermidine extends lifespan by inducing autophagy
claims.believers: T Nation articles state that animal models show lifespan extensions as large as 25 percent [2].
claims.experts: Lifespan extension is reported in yeast, flies, worms and mice, but evidence for lifespan effects in humans is lacking [6][7][5].

claims.claim: Eating wheat germ or other spermidine-rich foods is a practical way to get the benefit
claims.believers: T Nation writers recommend wheat germ as a spermidine source [2][3].
claims.experts: Observational studies link dietary polyamine intake with lower mortality, but they cannot establish causation and no trial has tested food-based dosing [4].

claims.claim: Spermidine improves memory and brain health
claims.believers: Supplement promotion cites animal cognition studies [15].
claims.experts: A randomised trial in older adults with subjective cognitive decline tested memory outcomes, and reviews describe human evidence as preliminary [8][4].

claims.believers: Wikipedia reports the lab observation that spermidine lengthened hair shafts in cultured follicles [1].
claims.experts: No clinical trial in humans has tested spermidine for hair growth.

claims.claim: Spermidine supports fertility and hormone balance
claims.believers: Wikipedia reports that fertile men have higher spermidine levels than infertile men, and the claim circulates in supplement marketing.[1]
claims.experts: The Wikipedia statement is tagged as needing medical citation, and no randomised trial of spermidine for human fertility appears in the literature reviewed here.[1]

claims.claim: Spermidine boosts immunity and vaccine response in older adults
claims.believers: Promoters point to its role in immune cell metabolism and eIF5A hypusination.[13]
claims.experts: A 2026 pilot randomised study examined immune cell senescence and vaccine responses in healthy older adults and a 40-person vaccination trial is registered; reviews describe the immune findings as largely preclinical.[18][19][13]

claims.claim: Spermidine is a caloric-restriction mimetic that does the work of fasting
claims.believers: Longevity writers on T Nation list it alongside resveratrol as a compound that recreates calorie-restriction benefits.[3]
claims.experts: The 2018 Science review uses the caloric-restriction-mimetic framing and says the effects were seen in rodent models and epidemiology; human intervention data are limited.[4]

angle.text: People take spermidine, usually as wheat germ or an extract, for longevity and healthy ageing. Its appearance link rests on a laboratory report that it lengthened hair shafts in cultured human follicles, and on the general idea of slowing age-related decline.
